listing.subtitle: Turn SVGs, text and pixel art into 3D
listing.description:
Draw pixel art, type a word in one of ten fonts, paste SVG code or drop an SVG file, and it stands up as a 3D object you can spin, light and dress in plastic, metal, glass, chrome, gold or wood.

Set its depth, smoothness and colour, choose a backdrop and an animation, and move the key light. Take a still up to 4K, transparent if you like, record a few loops as MP4 or WebM and trim them, or download the model as GLB, STL, OBJ or PLY for Blender, a game or a 3D printer.

It works without an account, and your design stays in the browser. Sign in to keep your shapes in My shapes, open them on any device, and share any one by a link that anyone can turn and copy, until you turn it off. A port of the open-source 3dsvg editor, with no build step.

apps.prompt:
Build a catalog as a Holm App Spec v1 app using only
https://holmhq.com/llms-full.txt for Holm; read sections 9–12 first. Use catalog/
with holm.json, public web/ files, api/main.js exporting
default { async fetch(request, env) }, standard Request/Response, env.holm
storage/auth and env.holm.web.fetch(request) fallback. No build step or
third-party runtime CDN; vendor fonts and any libraries with licenses.

- Define these repository conventions, not a claimed Holm store protocol:
  each top-level app has holm.json version, holm.symbol.svg (one black path,
  no strokes, 0 0 24 24) and listing/listing.json with subtitle, category,
  description, whatsNew and sample screenshots. Write a dependency-free
  Node scripts/index.mjs emitting root index.json: name/path/version,
  <app>/v<version> tag, h1 SHA-256 file fingerprint, size/count, identity,
  symbol path, listing and PROMPT text. Hash sorted app-relative paths and
  file SHA-256 values, then hash those “<hex>  <path>\n” lines and prefix
  the base64 digest with h1:. Exclude listing/ and hidden files; count README
  and PROMPT too. --check detects stale indexes or changed release tags;
  --tag creates missing tags. CI checks then tags versions on main.
- An App Store-like front page: a slideshow of the featured apps' cards
  (no controls; it holds under the mouse, and a mouse drags it),
  then all apps with search (as you type, kept in ?q=) and a list/grid
  switch below it; the grid is ruled like the facts strip (no boxes, lines
  meeting), each near-square cell the icon with its name centred under it,
  no Get and no hover zoom. Each app's own
  /apps/<app> page: icon/colour, version, size, category, license, swipeable
  screenshots, description, whatsNew with a folded version history (the
  index's history: each earlier tag's whatsNew and date), and source
  information. Keep each app's prompt in the index, but don't show it for
  now. The description's first paragraph (at most 300 characters, which
  --check enforces) is its short version, with More for the rest. With no
  reviews, show one slim strip whose stars open the review form. End with
  four related apps (named in listing.json "related", then the same
  category) and See all, so every page ends at the same place.
- The index also carries each app's MCP tools from its api/contract.json
  (name, summary, risk, auth). An app with tools gets an MCP pill beside
  Get that opens a Connect via MCP sheet: the app's icon joined to the MCP
  mark by five waving dots, a click-to-copy connector address
  (https://<host>/_holm/mcp) with two small index tabs on its top edge,
  Demo (the repository's running copy, when signed-in people may use the
  tools; Claude's sign-in there makes an account) and Your node (the host
  from the Get sheet), then tabs for Claude, ChatGPT and Claude Code steps
  and the tools grouped by risk. The sheet never changes height.
  Read the public repository index with synchronous env.holm.net.fetch,
  not global fetch; cache it in KV and keep the last good index on failure.
- Make it fast: the handler serves every page with the index and the viewer
  embedded, so the first paint waits on no API call (Holm serves a matching
  static file first, so don't name the shell index.html), and preload every
  module. Give each
  /apps/<app> page that app's title, description and listing/cover.png as
  its link preview (a 1200x630 card the repo draws with a script).
- Get opens a sheet remembering my peer/domain, with tabs for
  holm @<peer> app install github.com/<org>/<repo>/<app>@v<version> --host
  <host>, a clone-a-tag holm app deploy <app> --spec-v1, and an agent prompt
  following the app README.
- A /start guide, linked from a header button that stands out and the sheet, for
  someone with no node who will hand the work to a coding agent, never a
  terminal: what Holm is, why a node puts every app here one request away,
  then pick an app and where it runs (this computer, a server, an existing
  node) for a prompt to paste, what the agent asks (the licence is always
  the person's to accept), and the commands folded away. Then building from
  a prompt, what Holm gives an app, links to holmhq.com. Keep it airy.
  Beside its headline, vendor an MIT isometric line-figure kernel and draw
  an interactive figure on it: the apps ride a belt as crates from a store,
  through a gate (the fingerprint check), into a node drum; pointing slows
  the belt and names the crate's app.
- web/llms.txt for that agent: ground rules, the index, and setup, install,
  sign-in and server steps citing sections 4, 5, 8, 9 and 13 of the guide.
  The sheet's agent prompt comes first.
- Sign in through Holm. Signed-in people may rate/review once per app;
  edits wait for approval too. /admin hides apps, moderates reviews, shows
  rough daily views/Get/copy counts in KV and lets me change the tint.
  Authorize each route with documented isAppOwner()/isAppAdmin() checks.
  The guide does not document isNodeOwner()/isNodeAdmin(): do not assume
  those methods or promise node-role access for a fresh build.
- The guide does not document binary net.fetch responses: do not invent
  responseType: 'file'. Keep screenshots as public static files in web/
  until a documented, tested proxy/cache path is available; disclose that
  gap. Make light/dark mobile/desktop layouts, no sideways scrolling, and a
  fixed shell: the window never scrolls, one panel does, under a header that
  frosts once the page runs under it and a small Holm/source footer that
  stays at the bottom, frosted. A versioned service worker keeps every file
  and the front page; pages open from it and redraw only if the API says
  something changed. The avatar menu (a second tap closes it) has a light/dark/
  same-as-device switch, kept in the browser and applied before first
  paint, and Analytics from __HOLM_SURFACES__.

Check the peer/unused host and explicitly allow the repository's egress host;

listing.subtitle: Decks you make with Claude, for your team
listing.description:
Make a workspace for your team, connect Claude, and ask for a deck. Claude drafts, tightens and rearranges, and every save lands in the deck you have open, on the slide you were looking at, with a note saying what changed.

Seven layouts keep every deck looking considered: a cover with a fan of what comes next, a statement with a highlighted phrase, cards, a flow, a screenshot with boxes and pins, numbers that count up, and the ask with owners and dates. There is no free canvas to make a mess on.

Edit words right on the slide, or every detail in the inspector: lists of cards and steps, links, colours, the picture, speaker notes. Drag slides into order, change a slide's layout without losing its words, and pick one of six accents for the deck. Every save is kept, so any earlier version can come back.

Invite teammates with a link. Decks and the picture library stay private to the workspace until you share one: a link that follows your latest save or stays on one version, and an embed for any website. Present with keys, swipes, notes and a clock, on a big screen or a phone, or print one slide per page.
listing.whatsNew: Deck opens at once and stays still: it keeps its files on your device, draws your decks, library and team from what it last saw, and Decks, Library and Team keep their place as you move between them. ⌘K jumps to a place, a deck or an action. Share one link and let people book time with you: no account for them, no app, no back-and-forth. Guests pick a time on a strip of your free days, or paint when they’re free and you choose.

Your page lives at your own address, like /@avery, with your photo, what you do, your website and profiles, and a link for each kind of meeting you offer, each showing the next time that's open. Give your pages one of six colours, each made for light and for dark, and a link that shares with a cover of your name and photo, or an image of your own.

Your free time lies on a strip of days, time running left to right like a video editor's timeline. Guests tap a shaded span and the meeting drops in, the length of the event; they drag it along the day and it snaps to the times that are open. If nothing suits them, they paint when they're free instead, even outside your hours, and where it meets your free time it glows. You see their times over your own week, drag the meeting to a time inside them and accept, or say no with a note.

Both of you get an email whose calendar invite puts the meeting on your calendar. The guest can move or cancel with the link in their email. Paint your weekly hours on the same kind of strip, trimming and sliding spans like clips, even onto another day, where they trade places with what's in the way; drag a day over another and the two swap as you go. Pause a day with a switch, zoom the day in and out, and keep days off. Guests see times in their own zone, with daylight saving handled on both sides.

Insights show page views, visitors, profile clicks, bookings, time on page, where visitors came from, what they used and where they are, without cookies. Tracked links tag your page for a flyer, a newsletter or a talk, each with a QR code, and show which one brought each visit and booking. And you can run all of it from Claude: connect its MCP connector and it can change your profile, hours and event types, list meetings, answer requests and read your insights.

listing.description:
Send SMS through the Android phone in your pocket, from any browser or from your own scripts. Install the free SMS Gateway for Android app, paste the username and password it shows, and your texts go out on your own SIM and plan. People see your own number, and their replies come back here.

Every text shows its time and ticks: one when your phone sends it, two when it's delivered, and a clear note with Try Again when it doesn't get through. Name the people you text, send to up to ten at once, pick a SIM, send later, and fill in templates you use often. A ring counts how much of an SMS you've used as you type. Replies and receipts arrive live, with quiet sounds you can turn off.

It feels at home on a phone, with a tab bar, sheets that slide up and a swipe to go back, and on a computer, with your conversations beside the open one and keyboard shortcuts.

A personal SIM stays personal: Zend asks before sending anything that reads like an offer or a one-time code, stays under India's limits for bulk texts, and honours every STOP. API keys can be held to a few numbers, so a key that leaks can't text anyone else. No phone handy? A demo phone pretends to send, deliver and reply.

Press ⌘K to jump to a conversation, a tab or Connect via MCP, and / to search your chats. The footer has a Feedback link: tell us what you think in a short form without leaving the app. Admins see Analytics in the account menu right after signing in.

apps.prompt:
Build "Zend", an app for texting from your own Android phone, using only
https://holmhq.com/llms-full.txt for Holm. Read its v1 sections 9–12 and
"Make an app feel finished" and "Make it feel native" first. Make
holm.json, public web/ files and api/main.js exporting default
{ async fetch(request, env) }. Set web.spa true, use env.holm for storage,
sign-in, outbound HTTP, secrets and realtime, return standard Responses and
fall back to env.holm.web.fetch(request). No build step or third-party
runtime CDN; vendor the font and icons with their licences.

- After sign-in, each member connects their own phone running SMS Gateway
  for Android (https://sms-gate.app, cloud mode): they paste its username,
  password and, for live receipts, its webhook signing key. Check them
  against SMSGate's public API through env.holm.net, never show them again,
  and keep them encrypted under a VAULT_KEY runtime secret. Offer a demo
  phone that pretends to send, deliver and reply, so anyone can try it.
- Conversations per number, with names, unread replies, search, an SMS-part
  counter (GSM-7 and Unicode), up to 10 numbers per text, SIM choice,
  templates with blanks, and scheduled texts that can be cancelled. Show
  each text's state as ticks: sent, then delivered. Register the phone's
  webhooks and verify each one's HMAC signature, timestamp and envelope id.
- Keep a personal SIM personal, as India's SMS rules (TRAI's TCCCPR 2018 and
  its 2025 and 2026 amendments) require: a declaration when a phone is
  connected; texts that read like OTPs or offers need confirming on the
  page and are refused by the API; stop at TRAI's "bulk" counts of same or
  similar texts; cap texts and different people per day; honour STOP
  replies with an opt-out list. Templates use DLT's {#var#} blanks.
- API keys for the member's own scripts: shown once, stored as a hash,
  optionally held to a few numbers, with the same limits and an
  Idempotency-Key for safe retries.
- MCP tools as named operations in api/contract.json with auth "user", each
  reaching only the caller's own data: conversations and unread replies,
  reading one, marking it read, naming a number, the phone and today's
  limits, templates, and drafts. Tools never send. A draft waits at the top
  of Chats, live, until the person opens it, checks it and taps Send, or
  discards it; drafts go after a day. Connect via MCP… in the account menu,
  with the MCP mark, opens a sheet with the connector address to click and
  copy, and tabs for Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code and what the tools do.
- An exquisite UI that feels like Apple's Messages or Telegram, on a phone
  and on a desktop: a tab bar on phones, a rail with the conversation list
  beside the open conversation on wide screens, frosted bars, large titles,
  bubbles with tails and the time inside, sheets that slide up, a round
  avatar account button even when signed out, whose menu closes when it's
  tapped again and holds light/dark/auto as three icons (Holm branding stays
  in the footer at the end of each tab), motion and quiet sounds. ⌘K opens
  a command menu of tabs, conversations and actions, Connect via MCP…
  among them. Installable, with a versioned service worker that keeps every
  page file and opens the app from them; the conversation list draws at
  once from the last launch's copy, which sign-out clears.
- For this repository's store, use holm.json version, holm.symbol.svg (one
  black path, no strokes, 0 0 24 24) and listing/listing.json with subtitle,
  category, description, whatsNew and sample screenshots. These are repo
  conventions, not a catalog format promised by the Holm guide.

Run holm app validate --spec-v1 zend. With my approval, deploy with
holm @<peer> app deploy zend --spec-v1 --host zend.<my-domain>, then ask
before allowing api.sms-gate.app for the app and setting VAULT_KEY. Never
replace an occupied host without asking. Validation does not run the app:
test the demo phone, every refusal, two members, API keys, and signed,
unsigned, stale and repeated webhooks, on mobile and desktop in light and
dark, and sign in and out as a real person would. Check that code shared by
the page and the server gives the same answers in both. Report gaps
honestly. Inspect the target settings schema before setting sign-in
branding.
